questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to reason about 128-bit bit patterns and leverage existing helper functions to implement non-trivial properties without using conditional branches.

## Key Concepts
- Bit reversal and palindrome detection in 128-bit space
- Constant-time, branchless implementation
- Integration with existing `reverse128` utility

## Code Example
```c
int isPalindrome128(uint64_t hi, uint64_t lo) {
  uint64_t rhi, rlo;
  reverse128(hi, lo, &rhi, &rlo);
  return (rhi == hi && rlo == lo);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this approach to 256-bit values?
- What optimizations could be applied if the function were called frequently?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests branchless bitwise selection across a 128-bit value. It mirrors practical use cases like compositing two 128-bit values with a mask in a single pass.

## Key Concepts

- Branchless bitwise selection
- 128-bit composition via hi/lo fields
- Handling of full-range masks across both lanes

## Code Example

```c
uint128 blend128(uint128 a, uint128 b, uint128 mask) {
  uint128 t1 = and128(a, mask);
  uint128 t2 = and128(b, not128(mask));
  return or128(t1, t2);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate correctness across all 2^128 mask patterns efficiently?
- How would this approach extend to 256-bit operands with the same interface?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of efficient, branchless bit tricks and how to detect patterns across bit ranges.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless computation
- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Pattern detection in fixed width integers

## Code Example
```javascript
function hasAdjacentOnes32(x) {
  return (x & (x >>> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a generic width W? 
- How would you test edge cases (all zeros, all ones, alternating patterns) and discuss performance implications?
